sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve that rises and settles.
sections.body_md:
State-space models apply to any system with stored quantities. A tank stores liquid, so the level is the state. A motor stores angular momentum, so the speed is the state. A pendulum stores energy in position and velocity, so it has two states.

The modeling process is the same: identify the stored quantities, write the balance laws, and package them as \(\dot{x} = Ax + Bu\). The parameters change (tank area instead of inertia, hydraulic resistance instead of damping), but the structure is the same. This lets you reuse the same analysis tools across domains.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Tank: \(\dot{h} = \dfrac{q_{in}}{A} - \dfrac{h}{AR}\). Time constant \(\tau = AR\).

Motor: \(\dot{\omega} = \dfrac{K_t i}{J} - \dfrac{b\omega}{J}\). Time constant \(\tau = J/b\).

Pendulum (linearized near downward): \(\ddot{\theta} + \dfrac{g}{\ell}\theta = 0\). Natural frequency \(\omega_n = \sqrt{g/\ell}\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A tank has area \(A = 3\) m\(^2\) and hydraulic resistance \(R = 5\) s/m\(^2\). The time constant is \(\tau = 3 \times 5 = 15\) s. With inflow \(q_{in} = 0.6\) m\(^3\)/s, the equilibrium level is \(h_e = q_{in} R = 0.6 \times 5 = 3\) m. The state-space coefficient is \(-1/(AR) = -1/15 = -0.0667\). Using the area or the resistance alone as the time constant is wrong; the time constant is their product.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Different domains use different symbols for the same concept. The time constant is \(J/b\) for a motor and \(AR\) for a tank, but both are the ratio of storage capacity to dissipation. Confusing the input with the state (like calling the inflow a state) gives the wrong model. The linearized pendulum is valid only for small angles; large swings break the approximation.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Realization writes a transfer function as a state-space model. Discrete-time models sample the continuous model at fixed intervals. Linearization builds a linear model around an operating point of a nonlinear system. All of these steps start with the state-space form that this skill introduces.
